Bunkering - disaster waiting to happen

By: Liz Fish | Paid

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
There is a disaster in the making in Algoa Bay just outside Gqeberha. Since 2016 ship-to ship transfer of oil or bunkering as it is known- has happened in open waters adjacent the Addo National Park Marine Protected Area (MPA) and within the natural foraging zones of endangered and IUCN Red Listed bird species. Anchorage 2 is located on the boundary of the Addo MPA which and close to St Croix Island which previously held the largest African penguin breeding colony in the world, and Bird Island currently holds the world’s largest Cape gannet breeding colony, with two thirds of the global population breeding at this site. In 5 years the penguin population has dropped from 23 000 to 3000 on St Croix Island 80%, three times higher than the decline at Bird Island

Summary:
On Monday 23 May 3000 litres of low sulphur oil were spilt in a ship to ship transfer of oil after a pipe burst. This is the second spill in a month, on the 23 April 2022 the spill resulted in oiled seabirds having to be retrieved from Bird Island on 3 May. Another oil leak was detected by vessel tracking, in the same area and has thus far been unreported. This is the third sizeable oil spill since operations began six years ago and environmentalists fear the smaller oil spills are not being reported.
The clean-up continued over four days assisted by spotter aircraft tracking the oil drift towards the sensitive bird islands. If a relatively small spill took 4 days to clear it raises the question does SAMSA have the resources to cope with oil spills and what happens if there is a larger spill? Marine fuel is classified as hazardous to aquatic environment with a specific hazard statement of very toxic to aquatic life, with long-lasting effects.
Sea birds forage over a wide range and the bay is full of pelagic fish at the moment and the clean up vessels had substantial hull oil deposits which still have to be cleaned up. Bunkering should happen without any oil spills, but pipes are being connected in open waters in all weather conditions. The added concern is that at any one time there are 20 to 30 vessels in the bay and all their bilge water containing cleaning chemicals and sewerage is disposed of in the Bay.


Further information:
The latest spill was substantially greater because the pumping and transfer rate was much higher, the mothership tanker Umnenga II holding capacity is 95 millions litres of fuel oil and the smaller vessel Lefkas 6320 litres. Ship to ship bunkering can best be described as a fuel station as sea that dispenses marine fuel oils that are hazardous and toxic and in vast quantities. Estimates of the value of bunker fuel being transferred in Algoa Bay exceed R5.0 billion per annum ( at oil prices Dec 2021) with most of the benefits flowing to international oil suppliers. Many fuel transfer vessels are hired on charter and the crews are not local.
Penguins are indicative species, and with such a drastic decline in numbers that we are witnessing, signifies a very impacted and unfavourable environment. It indicates that something is very wrong in the ecosystem. This is an unsustainable situation, with the penguin population on St Croix Island facing extinction within the next few years.

Marine eco-tourism has grown because of the unspoilt nature of the Bay. Estimates place a value on eco-tourism with a healthy Algoa Bay as in excess of R6 billion per annum. In addition, the commercial and recreational fishery rely heavily on a healthy MPA to secure the effective spawning of and nursery for many of the marine species.
There was a moratorium on awarding new bunkering licences until a proper risk assessment could be done and the completion of the holding capacity. In January, Samsa announced that the moratorium on the awarding of bunkering licences would be lifted from 1 April. Environmentalist managed to holt the issuing of new licences but after Mondays spill they are calling for a complete halt until a full EIA and public participation process has been undertaken

There is a legal loop hole in the MPLRA Act which does not require an EIA at sea because when the Act was drawn up there was no bunkering off shore in SA. An EIA id required on land for any fuel station to be established. I bunker which holds over 90 million litres. However the Minister of Environment can stop the activity if it is polluting the waters.



Extra Budget Items:
Pay for boat trip around Algoa Bay and out to St Croix and Bird Island and we will have to fly in Wednesday because of lack of flights and we have to be at sea early THursday

Script:


Script: On a blustery Gqueberha afternoon, we’re heading to sea with marine conservationist, Lloyd Edwards. For the past 30 years, he’s enthralled visitors to Algoa Bay with sightings of whales, Bottlenose Dolphins, sea birds and, of course, African Penguins at the famous colony on St Croix Island. But, we’re on the lookout for something else …its called bunkering
Derek: Get it off your chest. Tell us what you think of bunkering
Lloyd: Well, Derek, ….this is the most serious threat that's faced Algoa bay in the 30 years that I have been doing this.
Script: Bunkering is ship-to-ship refuelling that occurs at sea rather than in port, and it’s raised alarm bells for those concerned about its impact on nature.
As we head out 10 vessels are already visible on the horizon. It doesn’t take long to spot the first refuelling ship
LINK This is really the petrol attendant - a bunker barge that gets fuelled from the mother ship and then heads off to fuel the customers which are passing cargo ships
Script: The mother ship is carrying 90 million litres of fuel. Lloyds estimates that's the equivalent of just under 1000 petrol stations and it’s sitting right on top of a marine protected area. Over 100 vessels are refuelled this way each month.
Derek: If you go back more than five years. Were there alarm bells ringing when you heard about this boat coming so close to shore.
Lloyd: Yeah, definitely the alarm bells were ringing, but of course, we were assured that it would not effect the penguins. We've got almost 100% safety record in the Mediterranean. This is not the Mediterranean. This is Algoa Bay this is big westerly winds. This is big storms. You know, you can't compare the two.
Script: Ship to ship bunkering started in 2016 when our government spotted a gap in the market: the 1000’s of ships passing our coastline were getting caught in bottlenecks as they approached port to refuel. It’s fallen to the Marine Safety Authority, SAMSA, a government agency, to ensure the refuelling at sea is done safely. Captain Vernon Keller says weather is just one of many factors considered.
Keller The bunkering is not a wild, wild west story out there. There are set international process and procedures that need to be followed globally. These vessels are managed via what we call a safety management system, and those are set procedures when you connect and you disconnect
Script: That’s cold comfort to some conservationists who insist the practice is damaging nature.
LINK When bunkering started there were around 23000 penguins on St Croix island here about 4kms offshore and now today we spotted about half a dozen and it’s really tragic and it makes you wonder what we are doing to our marine environment
Script: The reasons for the demise of St Croix’s penguins are complex, and few know that better than Professor Lorein Pichegru who’s spent the past 15 years trying to get to the bottom of it.
Lorien Recently they've been decreasing over the past seven years by 90%.
Derek: By 90%
Lorien: 90% yeah
Script: It’s a figure made more shocking by research that shows penguins don’t migrate. So, despite the threat posed by two nearby harbours and signs of diminishing fish stocks, they won’t leave their colony on St Croix.
Lorien: For the past two years we were wondering how penguins could decrease that fast?
Script: Their attention turned to another - less obvious – type of pollution.
Lorien So the latest research showed the noise levels from maritime traffic over eight years, so we measured before bunkering and after bunkering. Algoa Bay is one of the noisiest bays in the world.
Script: An astonishing finding considering it’s nowhere near the biggest. Attaching hydrophones, her team measured the penguins’ communication patterns
Lorien: Penguins talk on the surface. So they work together underwater to create baitballs to forage, but they need to coordinate themselves just like dolphins.
Upsound of dolphins
Lorien Noise pollution underwater in the oceans is something we started to realise internationally only 12 or 15 years ago. So it's not only whales and dolphins, a lot of fish are using sound to find a mate, to find food, to avoid predators. So we are messing with that environment and affecting their lives in ways we don't understand.
Script: And speaking of “messing”, while it may not explain the loss of penguins, bunkering presents another threat to the environment
LINK There have been numerous oil spills since bunkering began here around 6 years ago and considering the number of ships being refuelled, it’s bound to happen again.
Script: In the last oil spill the pipe burst and it’s pumping 150 000 litres a minute. Chemist Ronell Friend has been campaigning to raise public awareness of its dangers
Ronell: This is classed as an environmental toxin. it has a long duration that it can have toxicity. And in one of the operator’s safety data sheets they actually state that it bio accumulates in the marine environment
Script: And the oil’s high sulphur content means Penguins are confused into thinking its nourishment.
Ronell: What is happening with this oil, with high sulphur ….it's simulates food for them. ……penguins come swimming around, diving into the oil because they think there is food.
Script: And oil and feathers are a deadly mix: in the 1st spill 100’s of oiled birds were removed from the islands and many more no doubt died at sea. Aidan Bellingan is from SANCCOB - the Foundation for Conservation of Coastal Birds. Oil spills are their worst nightmare
Derek: What would happen to a bird that was left oiled up on its nests on one of these islands?
Adian: It would probably starve to death. So once a birds oiled, it's a struggle to swim because it gets cold so it would either die out at sea or it would die onland just because it's too cold to regulate its body temperature.
Script: And when they return to their nests the oil suffocates their eggs and chicks, so they too are removed. Rehabilitating an oiled bird is an extremely delicate process.
Adian With very potent oils like diesel, for example, we washed the bird immediately because diesel is extremely toxic to the birds and it burns the bird. Washing is extremely intense process for the birds and it's very hard on them and their hearts. If we aren't keeping a close eye on them with the waterproofing, they can also die of hypothermia.
Script: After the spill in 2019, SANCCOB successfully argued for a moratorium on the issuing of new bunkering licences until a full risk assessment was done. It has yet to happen.
Keller says in his 30 years at sea, he never had an accident while refueling a ship- he thinks the environmental risks are exaggerated
Keller: If you look at it, over 6 billion litres of oil has been transferred and you've had less than 3000 litres spoiled in a six year period. That's a risk rating of 0.0005%.
Script: Keller says globally safety standards for ship-to-ship transfers have improved and SAMSA ensures they’re enforced, issuing heavy fines for any negligence. But high level suspensions on charges of misconduct and alleged bunkering contract irregularities, have cast a shadow over SAMSA’s credibility. None-the-less, six months ago, the agency announced it was accepting new licencing applications

Derek: But surely the safety of the environment comes first to say, why can't we do this risk assessment?
Keller: the risk assessment was supposed to be done by the port authorities. And basically the reason it was a decision to lift the moratorium,…. And also the TNPA, the Port Authority could not tell us at what timeline they will complete the actual risk assessment. And we had a lot of South African companies also lining up to be able to enter this market.
Script: But after a public outcry the moratorium on new licences remained in place. With two more oil spills in the last few months conservation groups are now asking for bunkering to only happen in the harbours- to date they have had no response.
Lloyd Not all of that oil, heavy furnace, oil floats. So these guys are all trying to clean up the floating stuff. Most of it actually sinks. Some of it disperses into the water and other evaporates. ….. And of course, the government are now crowing. Oh, no, no birds got oiled,……The reason that no penguins got oiled is because there's almost none left
Script: We wrote to the Minister of Environment Barbara Creecy asking what she was doing to protect the endangered African penguin and the marine protected area against the impacts of bunkering.
We received no reply. But as bunkering is not a listed activity under the National Environmental Marine Act it does not require a full environmental impact assessment. She has previously said her department is working closely with SAMSA and the Port authorities to ensure the highest safety standards. But is it too little too late to help ease the pressure on the penguins?
Lorien What I would really like to see is St Croix being closed to fishing. There was never any effective closure for fishing. To this day, I mean, the minister promised to have a closure this year. We were promised some decisions for the past four or five years. Nothing has happened.
Lloyd: It just makes me so flipping sad to see who's going to pay for this demise. Who's accountable for this?

Script: And when they return to their nests the oil suffocates their eggs and chicks, so they too are removed. Rehabilitating an oiled bird is an extremely delicate process. Adian With very potent oils like diesel, for example, we washed the bird immediately because diesel is extremely toxic to the birds and it burns the bird. Washing is extremely intense process for the birds and it's very hard on them and their hearts. If we aren't keeping a close eye on them with the waterproofing, they can also die of hypothermia. Script: After the spill in 2019, SANCCOB successfully argued for a moratorium on the issuing of new bunkering licences until a full risk assessment was done. It has yet to happen. Keller says in his 30 years at sea, he never had an accident while refueling a ship- he thinks the environmental risks are exaggerated Keller: If you look at it, over 6 billion litres of oil has been transferred and you've had less than 3000 litres spoiled in a six year period. That's a risk rating of 0.0005%. Script: Keller says globally safety standards for ship-to-ship transfers have improved and SAMSA ensures they’re enforced, issuing heavy fines for any negligence. But high level suspensions on charges of misconduct and alleged bunkering contract irregularities, have cast a shadow over SAMSA’s credibility. None-the-less, six months ago, the agency announced it was accepting new licencing applications Derek: But surely the safety of the environment comes first to say, why can't we do this risk assessment? Keller: the risk assessment was supposed to be done by the port authorities. And basically the reason it was a decision to lift the moratorium,…. And also the TNPA, the Port Authority could not tell us at what timeline they will complete the actual risk assessment. And we had a lot of South African companies also lining up to be able to enter this market. Script: But after a public outcry the moratorium on new licences remained in place. With two more oil spills in the last few months conservation groups are now asking for bunkering to only happen in the harbours- to date they have had no response. Lloyd Not all of that oil, heavy furnace, oil floats. So these guys are all trying to clean up the floating stuff. Most of it actually sinks. Some of it disperses into the water and other evaporates. ….. And of course, the government are now crowing. Oh, no, no birds got oiled,……The reason that no penguins got oiled is because there's almost none left Script: We wrote to the Minister of Environment Barbara Creecy asking what she was doing to protect the endangered African penguin and the marine protected area against the impacts of bunkering. We received no reply. But as bunkering is not a listed activity under the National Environmental Marine Act it does not require a full environmental impact assessment. She has previously said her department is working closely with SAMSA and the Port authorities to ensure the highest safety standards. But is it too little too late to help ease the pressure on the penguins? Lorien What I would really like to see is St Croix being closed to fishing. There was never any effective closure for fishing. To this day, I mean, the minister promised to have a closure this year. We were promised some decisions for the past four or five years. Nothing has happened. Lloyd: It just makes me so flipping sad to see who's going to pay for this demise. Who's accountable for this?

metadata.Unique Selling Point: There is a disaster in the making in Algoa Bay just outside Gqeberha. Since 2016 ship-to ship transfer of oil or bunkering as it is known- has happened in open waters adjacent the Addo National Park Marine Protected Area (MPA) and within the natural foraging zones of endangered and IUCN Red Listed bird species. Anchorage 2 is located on the boundary of the Addo MPA which and close to St Croix Island which previously held the largest African penguin breeding colony in the world, and Bird Island currently holds the world’s largest Cape gannet breeding colony, with two thirds of the global population breeding at this site. In 5 years the penguin population has dropped from 23 000 to 3000 on St Croix Island 80%, three times higher than the decline at Bird Island
metadata.Summary: On Monday 23 May 3000 litres of low sulphur oil were spilt in a ship to ship transfer of oil after a pipe burst. This is the second spill in a month, on the 23 April 2022 the spill resulted in oiled seabirds having to be retrieved from Bird Island on 3 May. Another oil leak was detected by vessel tracking, in the same area and has thus far been unreported. This is the third sizeable oil spill since operations began six years ago and environmentalists fear the smaller oil spills are not being reported. The clean-up continued over four days assisted by spotter aircraft tracking the oil drift towards the sensitive bird islands. If a relatively small spill took 4 days to clear it raises the question does SAMSA have the resources to cope with oil spills and what happens if there is a larger spill? Marine fuel is classified as hazardous to aquatic environment with a specific hazard statement of very toxic to aquatic life, with long-lasting effects. Sea birds forage over a wide range and the bay is full of pelagic fish at the moment and the clean up vessels had substantial hull oil deposits which still have to be cleaned up. Bunkering should happen without any oil spills, but pipes are being connected in open waters in all weather conditions. The added concern is that at any one time there are 20 to 30 vessels in the bay and all their bilge water containing cleaning chemicals and sewerage is disposed of in the Bay.
metadata.Further information: The latest spill was substantially greater because the pumping and transfer rate was much higher, the mothership tanker Umnenga II holding capacity is 95 millions litres of fuel oil and the smaller vessel Lefkas 6320 litres. Ship to ship bunkering can best be described as a fuel station as sea that dispenses marine fuel oils that are hazardous and toxic and in vast quantities. Estimates of the value of bunker fuel being transferred in Algoa Bay exceed R5.0 billion per annum ( at oil prices Dec 2021) with most of the benefits flowing to international oil suppliers. Many fuel transfer vessels are hired on charter and the crews are not local. Penguins are indicative species, and with such a drastic decline in numbers that we are witnessing, signifies a very impacted and unfavourable environment. It indicates that something is very wrong in the ecosystem. This is an unsustainable situation, with the penguin population on St Croix Island facing extinction within the next few years. Marine eco-tourism has grown because of the unspoilt nature of the Bay. Estimates place a value on eco-tourism with a healthy Algoa Bay as in excess of R6 billion per annum. In addition, the commercial and recreational fishery rely heavily on a healthy MPA to secure the effective spawning of and nursery for many of the marine species. There was a moratorium on awarding new bunkering licences until a proper risk assessment could be done and the completion of the holding capacity. In January, Samsa announced that the moratorium on the awarding of bunkering licences would be lifted from 1 April. Environmentalist managed to holt the issuing of new licences but after Mondays spill they are calling for a complete halt until a full EIA and public participation process has been undertaken There is a legal loop hole in the MPLRA Act which does not require an EIA at sea because when the Act was drawn up there was no bunkering off shore in SA. An EIA id required on land for any fuel station to be established. I bunker which holds over 90 million litres. However the Minister of Environment can stop the activity if it is polluting the waters.
